newsitem.title: CHINA: Rash of small listings seen damaging China markets.
newsitem.headline: Rash of small listings seen damaging China markets.

text.p: A flood of domestic A share listings is pulling down the overall quality of China's stock markets and undermining their development, analysts said on Friday.
A total of 121 new A share companies have listed on the exchanges in Shanghai and in Shenzhen since the start of 1996, raising the total of listed companies by about 40 percent.
But the companies listed this year are on average much smaller than those listed previously, which analysts said tended to make the market much more speculative.
The 68 new firms on the Shanghai stock exchange have on average only 27.1 million listed shares, against an average of 52 million shares for listed firms as of the end of 1995.
In Shenzhen, the 53 firms listed this year have on average 24.5 million listed shares against 66.2 million for listed firms at the end of 1995.

"Listing of a large number of small companies has damaged the healthy development of the markets," said one stock analyst with China Financial Trust and Investment Co. "This has also increased speculation in the market."

"Small firms are making the overall quality of companies on the two markets deteriorate," said another analyst with Shenyin & Wanguo Securities. "One of the major reasons is the existence of the share issue quota system."

Domestic share issues in China are decided by quotas that are distributed to provinces, major cities and industrial bureaux, with companies fighting ferociously to get the precious right to issue shares, stock analysts said.

In distributing the quota, some local governments or the bureaux divide it up between several companies to please them all rather than give all the shares to one big, high-quality firm and annoy the others, they said.
In the early years after China revived the stock markets in 1990, most listed companies were small, making the market extremely speculative and subject to wide fluctuations.

In 1993 and 1994, Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges selected major Chinese companies for listing, such as Shanghai Petrochemical Co and Maanshan Iron and Steel Co, to help improve the company composition.

"The latest batch of small firms has made company composition on the two markets deteriorate," said a broker with China Guotai Securities. "Cases of irregularities have also arisen, with firms competing for a slice of the quota system."
